name: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
title: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
answer: Valuing illiquid tokens covers the problem of putting a defensible number on a digital asset that has no reliable market price. It sits inside digital asset accounting, where holdings must be carried on a balance sheet, tested for impairment, or reported to a tax authority. The assets in question are tokens with thin order books, locked or vesting positions, tokens held by a project treasury, and positions in early stage networks. The work is not a single calculation but a documented judgement that has to survive an auditor's questions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Valuing illiquid tokens covers the problem of putting a defensible number on a digital asset that has no reliable market price. It sits inside digital asset accounting, where holdings must be carried on a balance sheet, tested for impairment, or reported to a tax authority. The assets in question are tokens with thin order books, locked or vesting positions, tokens held by a project treasury, and positions in early stage networks. The work is not a single calculation but a documented judgement that has to survive an auditor's questions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The inputs are whatever price evidence exists: trades on smaller exchanges, over the counter quotes, liquidity pool reserves, and the last round price paid by an investor. Teams pull this data through exchange APIs, on chain analytics tools, and portfolio trackers, then reconcile it against their own custody records. Spreadsheets and general ledger systems hold the working papers, and the valuation model itself is usually built in a spreadsheet rather than a dedicated pricing engine. The quality of the infrastructure matters less than whether the same sources are used consistently from period to period.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from an observable price and then adjust it for the things that make the token illiquid. Common adjustments cover the size of the holding relative to daily volume, lock up or vesting restrictions, and the discount a buyer would demand for a position that takes weeks to exit. Where no market price exists at all, valuation moves to a model, such as a discounted cash flow on network fees or a comparison to more liquid tokens with similar characteristics. Each input and each adjustment is written down with its source and its date, because the reasoning is as important as the final figure. Sensitivity testing, showing how the number moves when a key assumption changes, is standard practice.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The governing framework is a mix of accounting standards, tax rules, and fund valuation obligations, and the treatment differs depending on whether the holder is a company, a fund, or an individual. Auditors expect a written policy that sets out which pricing sources are acceptable, how often valuations are refreshed, and who signs off. Independence matters, so the person who trades the token should not be the only person who values it. Records need to show provenance: where each price came from, when it was captured, and what was known at the time. This is a description of how the work is done, not advice on any particular holding or filing.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more structured evidence and more automation of the data gathering. On chain data is becoming richer, which makes it easier to show real trading depth rather than a single quoted price. Regulators and standard setters continue to push for clearer disclosure of how illiquid positions are valued and what assumptions sit behind them. The harder problem, which is unlikely to disappear, is that a valuation is a point in time estimate for an asset whose price can move sharply, so the discipline of documenting the reasoning will keep mattering more than the precision of any single number.
